197.title: Sins first (Mark 2:1–12)
197.hook: the paralyzed man hears his sins forgiven before he hears walk
197.tomorrow: the sabbath was made for man
197.howItsDone: Catholics receive forgiveness in the sacrament of reconciliation, or confession, where a priest speaks the words of absolution; this gospel is read at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a leper knelt, and Jesus was moved, splanchnistheis, from the gut. Your line was he touched him. Today, four friends and a hole in a roof.

Jesus is back in Capernaum, word gets around, and the house is so packed there's no room even at the door. Four men arrive carrying their friend on a mat. He can't walk. They can't get in. So they do what good friends do when the front door fails: they climb onto the flat roof, dig a hole straight through it, and lower him down on ropes, right in front of Jesus, while dust and bits of roof fall on everybody's heads. Everyone knows what the man needs. And Jesus says something nobody expects.
screen: `A PACKED HOUSE.` → `FOUR FRIENDS ON THE ROOF.` → `A HOLE, AND A MAT ON ROPES.`

segments.voice: First, whose faith. Mark says Jesus saw their faith, the friends' faith. The man on the mat hasn't said a word; somebody else's trust carried him in. Second, the surprise. Jesus looks at him and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Not get up. Not be healed. Forgiven. The friends must have looked at each other: that's not what we came for. Third, the scribes. Some teachers of the law sit there, thinking it silently: "Why doth this man speak thus? he blasphemeth. Who can forgive sins, but God only?" In one way, they've understood exactly. Only God can forgive sins against God, and that's the point Mark wants you to feel. Then Jesus asks: which is easier, to say your sins are forgiven, or to say get up and walk? Anyone can say the first; nobody can check it. So, to show that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he tells the man: arise, take up thy bed, and go home. And he does, in front of everyone. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. Jesus never says the man's sin caused his paralysis; the gospels push back against that idea elsewhere. The story is about order: the deeper healing first, the one nobody could see. Catholics hear in this story the root of confession. They believe Christ gave his apostles a share in this power to forgive, and that it continues in the sacrament of reconciliation today.

198.title: The sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:13–28)
198.hook: he eats with sinners and says rest serves people, not the reverse
198.howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day by attending Mass and resting from unnecessary work, and the Church teaches that Sunday rest is meant for family, prayer and care for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sins first: a man through a roof, forgiven before he walked. Your line was the deeper healing first. Today, a dinner and a day of rest.

A day off, and the laptop is open on the couch. Chores get done so the day counts for something. "I'm resting," said like an apology. Rest can start to feel like a reward nobody has quite earned. In today's reading, Jesus gets into two arguments: one about who he eats dinner with, one about a day of rest and what it's for. And he settles it with one sentence.
screen: `A DAY OFF, FULL OF GUILT.` → `TWO ARGUMENTS.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETTLES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the dinner. Jesus walks past a tax collector named Levi, sitting at his booth, and says follow me, and Levi does. Mark sets tax collectors right beside sinners, which tells you how people saw them. Jesus eats at Levi's house with a crowd of tax collectors and sinners, and people object. He answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "They that are well have no need of a physician, but they that are sick." Second, the word. Sabbath is the Hebrew shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease. In Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and the commandments tell Israel to keep it holy and to let everyone rest: children, servants, foreigners, even the animals. Third, the argument. On a sabbath, Jesus's disciples pluck heads of grain as they walk through a field. Some Pharisees object that this is work. What counts as work was a real question in Jewish teaching, asked seriously. Jesus answers with a story about David, who ate the holy bread when his men were hungry. Then the sentence: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift for people, not a burden laid on them. Jewish teachers said something very close; a later rabbinic teaching puts it: the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. Fourth, what Catholics do with it. Christians came to gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and Catholics keep it as the Lord's Day: Mass, and rest from needless work.

199.title: The twelve (Mark 3:1–19)
199.hook: a withered hand healed, then he names twelve to be with him
199.howItsDone: Catholics keep feast days for each of the apostles through the year, and profess in the Creed that the Church is apostolic, led by bishops understood as the apostles' successors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath, made for people. Your line was rest is for you. Today, one more sabbath, and then a list of names.

Twelve names, read out on a hillside. Teams usually get picked for what people can do: speed, skill, good ideas. Here, Jesus climbs a hill, calls the ones he wants, and they come. He chooses twelve, and Mark lists every one by name. But before saying what they'll do, Mark says what they were chosen for first, and it isn't a skill.
screen: `PICKED FOR A SKILL?` → `ONE HILL, TWELVE NAMES.` → `CHOSEN FOR WHAT?`

segments.voice: First, a hand. On another sabbath, in a synagogue, there's a man whose hand is withered, and people watch to see what Jesus will do. He asks them, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy?" Nobody answers. Mark says Jesus looked round at them with anger, grieved, the Douay says, for the blindness of their hearts. Then he says to the man: stretch forth thy hand. And it's restored. Second, the hill. Jesus goes up a mountain and calls those he wants, and they come. "And he made that twelve should be with him, and that he might send them to preach." Some readers hear in the number the twelve tribes of Israel, a people being gathered again. Third, the order. First, to be with him. Then, to be sent. Before any preaching or healing, the job is to be with him: walk the roads, eat at the same fire, watch him pray at dawn. Fourth, the names. Simon, whom he names Peter. James and John, whom he nicknames sons of thunder. Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddeus, Simon the Cananean, and Judas Iscariot, who, Mark says right away, would betray him. Fishermen you've already met, two brothers nicknamed for thunder, and one named, right in the list, as the betrayer. Apostle is Greek, apostolos, one who is sent. Catholics believe the bishops today are the apostles' successors, a line that runs, they say, all the way back to that hill.

200.title: Who is my mother (Mark 3:20–35)
200.hook: his relatives come; he says whoever does God's will is his family; Catholics read brethren as kin, as Aramaic allows
200.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary as the first and most faithful disciple, and call one another brothers and sisters in Christ; the Church teaches Mary's perpetual virginity and reads the Lord's brethren as his relatives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve, the first apostles. Your line was first, to be with him. Today, day two hundred: two hundred days of showing up.

Someone in a family starts doing something the rest don't understand. Quits the job. Joins something. Moves away. And the relatives start talking: is he all right? Has she lost it? Somebody should bring him home. The crowds are so thick he can't even eat. Mark says his own people hear about it and set out to take charge of him, because they're saying he's out of his mind. Then his mother and brothers arrive, stand outside, and send someone in to call him.
screen: `THE FAMILY STARTS TALKING.` → `HE'S OUT OF HIS MIND.` → `HIS MOTHER AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Mark tells this as a sandwich: family, an argument, family again. First, the middle. Scribes come down from Jerusalem and say Jesus drives out demons by the power of the devil. He answers with a picture: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Why would Satan fight Satan? Second, the doorway. Someone tells him: your mother and your brethren are outside, looking for you. He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is my mother and my brethren?" He looks around at the people sitting in a circle at his feet. "Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother." It can sound cold. It isn't a rejection; it's a widening, open now to anyone who does God's will. Third, Mary. Catholics notice that no one did God's will more fully than Mary, who said yes to God before Jesus was born. Saint Augustine said she was more blessed for being his disciple than for being his mother. So this saying doesn't push her out. She's its best example. Fourth, the brethren. Christians read who they are differently. Catholics believe Mary remained a virgin, and read brethren as relatives, kin, since the Bible can use brother for wider family; in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother. Orthodox tradition holds they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. A common Protestant reading takes them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Each reads the same verse carefully, and the text itself doesn't settle it.

201.title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–20)
201.hook: now read the parable with the explanation beside it
201.tomorrow: the seed that grows while you sleep
201.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and some use it for lectio divina, asking which kind of ground they are right now.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a family widened to everyone who does God's will. Your line was family by doing God's will. Today, a farmer you've met before.

A farmer flinging seed: some on the path, some on rock, some in thorns, some on good soil. You've met him before, back in the stories camp, in Matthew's gospel. That time, it was a story. Now, reading Mark straight through, he comes back in Mark's own words, and this time you can do what a good reader does: lay the story beside the explanation Jesus gives his friends afterward, and look closely at one kind of ground.
screen: `A FARMER FLINGING SEED.` → `NOW IN MARK'S WORDS.` → `STORY AND EXPLANATION, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The crowd is so big that Jesus gets into a boat and sits on the water, teaching the people on the shore. He begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hear ye: Behold, the sower went out to sow." Four kinds of ground. Seed on the path is eaten by birds. Seed on rock springs up fast and withers in the sun, with no root. Seed among thorns is choked. Seed on good ground yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. And he ends: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Second, the explanation. Later, alone with the twelve, Jesus explains it line by line. The seed is the word. The path is the person the word never gets into. The rock is the one who welcomes it with joy but falls away when trouble comes. Good ground is the one who hears, receives, and bears fruit. Third, the thorns, and there's nothing dramatic about them. "And the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts after other things entering in choke the word, and it is made fruitless." The thorns don't kill the seed on the first day. It sprouts. It grows. It's just slowly crowded out by worry, by money, by wanting other things, until nothing comes of it. Nobody decides to stop listening. It gets choked. Fourth, the harvest. Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: some readers hear that last number as astonishing to people who farmed. The parable ends not in failure but in abundance.

202.title: The seed that grows while you sleep (Mark 4:21–34)
202.hook: a lamp on its stand, and seed that grows though the sower doesn't know how
202.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parables of the growing seed and the mustard seed at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and often read them as a lesson in patience and trust in God's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower again, and the thorns that choke. Your line was the thorns are the cares. Today, more seeds, and a parable only Mark tells.

A bean in a paper cup at school, tomatoes on a balcony: if you've ever planted anything, you know the temptation. You check it every morning. You want to dig it up a little to see if anything's happening. You water it too much. Nothing you do makes it go faster. Then one day there's a green thread poking out of the dirt, and you didn't see it happen. It happened at night, or while you were at work, without you. Jesus told a parable about exactly that, and only Mark kept it.
screen: `A BEAN IN A PAPER CUP.` → `CHECKING EVERY MORNING.` → `IT GREW WITHOUT YOU.`

segments.voice: Jesus is still teaching from the boat, with a handful of short sayings and parables. First, the lamp. Nobody lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel basket or under a bed; you put it on the lampstand. What's hidden is meant to come to light. Second, the seed that grows by itself, only in Mark. In the Douay-Rheims: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, And should sleep, and rise, night and day, and the seed should spring, and grow up whilst he knoweth not." "For the earth of itself bringeth forth fruit, first the blade, then the ear, afterwards the full corn in the ear." Of itself: in Greek, automatē, the word English turned into automatic. Third, what it means. The farmer's work is real: he sows, and when it's ripe, he harvests. But the growing isn't his. Christians hear this about the kingdom of God, and about faith in a person's life: it grows in stages, often unseen, and it isn't all up to you. For anyone who worries they're not doing enough, that's a relief. Fourth, the mustard seed. The kingdom is like the smallest of seeds that becomes a plant so large birds can nest in its shade. Small beginnings, hidden growth, a surprising size. Mark says Jesus taught many parables like these, and explained everything privately to his disciples.

203.title: Peace, be still (Mark 4:35–41)
203.hook: reading the storm again: why are you fearful
203.howItsDone: Catholics hear the calming of the storm at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time; Pope Francis preached on this passage in an empty St. Peter's Square during the COVID-19 pandemic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seed that grows while you sleep, automatē, of itself. Your line was it grows while you sleep. Today, the same evening, out on the lake.

Evening, at the end of the same long day of parables. Jesus has been teaching from a boat, and he says, let's cross to the other side. They push off, just as they are. Then a great storm of wind rises, the waves beat into the boat, and it starts filling with water. Some of these men are fishermen; they know what a filling boat means. You've met this storm before, back in the stories. Read in Mark's order, you can see where it falls.
screen: `THE SAME LONG DAY.` → `LET US CROSS OVER.` → `A SUDDEN STORM.`

segments.voice: First, the sleeper. Mark gives a small, human detail. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he was in the hinder part of the ship, sleeping upon a pillow; and they awake him, and say to him: Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" A cushion in the stern, asleep after a day of teaching. And the disciples don't only ask for help. They ask, don't you care? Second, the command. He gets up, rebukes the wind, and says to the sea: "Peace, be still." In Mark's Greek, be still is literally be muzzled, the same word he used when Jesus silenced a demon in Capernaum. The wind stops, and there's a great calm. Third, the question to them. "Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Not yet. Mark's disciples are slow learners, and he doesn't hide it. Fourth, their question. Now they're more afraid than they were in the storm, and they say to each other: "Who is this (thinkest thou) that both wind and sea obey him?" That question is why the path just spent five weeks in the Psalms. There, it's God who rules the sea and stills its waves; one psalm tells of God turning a storm into a breeze. So when the wind obeys Jesus, the disciples are left staring at a question the psalms seem to answer. Mark doesn't answer it for them yet. He lets it hang there, in a quiet boat, in the dark.
screen: `ASLEEP ON A CUSHION.` · `PEACE, BE MUZZLED.` · `HAVE YOU NOT FAITH YET?` · `IN THE PSALMS, GOD RULES THE SEA.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS THAT BOTH WIND AND SEA OBEY HIM?`

segments.voice: Name this week's storm plainly, the bill, the diagnosis, the argument, the fear that wakes you, and picture it as wind and water in a small boat. If you pray, say the words into it slowly, peace, be still, as a prayer to Christ. If you don't, say them to yourself, to your own racing mind, and let your breath slow.
Peace. The first word Jesus speaks to the storm: peace, be still. And the calm that leaves the disciples asking who he is. Today's word.
Your line: who is this. The week ran from sins first, through the sabbath, the twelve, a widened family, the sower and the sleeping seed, to a storm the wind obeys. Day two hundred three, done.

chat.says: Why were the disciples more scared after Jesus calmed the storm?
options: In the psalms only God rules the sea, so they wondered: who is this?
They feared he'd be angry with them for waking him from his sleep.
They thought the calm was a trick and the storm would come back.
chat.meaning: When wind and sea obey him, the disciples ask who this is. In the psalms, it's God who stills the waves.
